plan.contextChunk: This figure plots Archimedes' spiral on a single polar grid across one full turn. The grid is a set of concentric gray circles about the origin crossed by gray radial spokes, with horizontal and vertical axes numbered by integers from -7 to 7 in both directions and tipped with arrowheads. A solid dark navy curve starts at the origin and sweeps counterclockwise, its distance from the center growing steadily as it goes, so the trace forms one open loop that never crosses itself and finishes on the positive horizontal axis at about six units out. Six filled black dots mark sample points along the curve, each tagged with an ordered pair whose two entries are equal: (pi/4, pi/4) just above and right of the origin, (pi/2, pi/2) directly above it near height 1.6, (pi, pi) out to the left at about three units, (5pi/4, 5pi/4) down and to the left, (7pi/4, 7pi/4) down and to the right, and (2pi, 2pi) at the loop's end on the right. Because the radius listed in each pair matches the angle listed beside it, the marked dots let the reader confirm the relation r = theta point by point, and the even widening of the loop between successive crossings of a given direction is what a radius growing in direct proportion to the swept angle looks like.

interactions.label: θ
interactions.teaches: At every position on the spiral, the distance from the origin matches the swept angle, so the polar coordinate is always of the form (θ, θ)

interactions.label: Trace the spiral
interactions.teaches: Archimedes' spiral comes from steady angular motion paired with steadily increasing radius, leaving a widening curve rather than a circle
Each labeled dot satisfies r = θ: clicking a point highlights both the angle direction and the circle whose radius equals that same value

demo_steps.title: Begin at the pole
demo_steps.narration: When θ = 0, the radius is also 0, so the spiral starts exactly at the origin. The moving point has not yet swept out any angle or distance.

demo_steps.title: Angle becomes radius
demo_steps.narration: As θ increases, the point rotates counterclockwise and moves outward at the same time. The readouts show that r and θ remain equal.

demo_steps.title: Check a labeled point
demo_steps.narration: Click a sample point such as (π, π): the highlighted ray gives the angle π, and the highlighted circle shows that the radius is also π.

demo_steps.title: Complete one full turn
demo_steps.narration: By θ = 2π, the point has returned to the positive horizontal direction, but it is now about 6.28 units from the origin instead of at the center.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: For r = θ, the angle swept and the radius grown are the same number, so one full rotation produces an outward-opening spiral rather than a closed circle.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a square polar-coordinate layout centered on the origin, with pale gray concentric circles and diagonal spokes behind bold black coordinate axes. Plot the spiral in dark navy from the origin, sweeping counterclockwise through one full turn and ending on the positive x-axis near radius 2π. Mark the six labeled black points at θ = π/4, π/2, π, 5π/4, 7π/4, and 2π, with labels placed close to the corresponding dots without covering the curve. The slider should move a prominent point along the same curve and update paired readouts for θ and r. Clicking a sample point should emphasize its radial ray and matching radius circle in a contrasting highlight color.

- Slider for theta: the learner drags theta from 0 to 2pi, the point travels along the spiral while the radius readout matches the angle readout, making the relation r = theta visible point by point.
- Animation for tracing the spiral: a rotating radius sweeps counterclockwise and leaves the curve behind as it lengthens, showing that Archimedes' spiral is produced by steady angular motion paired with steadily increasing distance from the origin.

Notice that the r-values are just the decimal form of the angle measured in radians. We can see them on a graph in the figure.

Archimedes’ spiral

Graph of Archimedes' spiral r=theta over [0,2pi]. Starts at origin and spirals out in one loop counterclockwise. Points (pi/4, pi/4), (pi/2,pi/2), (pi,pi), (5pi/4, 5pi/4), (7pi/4, pi/4), and (2pi, 2pi) are marked.
